claims.text: The alarm came shortly after midnight on 26 September 1983.
vo: just after midnight on september 26th 1983

claims.text: The early-warning computer reported a US missile launch to Petrov, the duty officer.
vo: a computer told one man that america had launched a nuclear missile

claims.text: The command centre was the Serpukhov-15 early-warning bunker near Moscow.
Weeks earlier (1 Sept 1983) the Soviet Union shot down KAL 007; all 269 aboard died.
claims.caveat: Reagan (5 Sept 1983): 'the Soviets scrambled jet interceptors', one pilot fired the missiles — so 'Soviet jets had shot down' is accurate shorthand. Prefer 'a Soviet fighter' in future scripts.
vo: weeks earlier soviet jets had shot down a passenger plane
two hundred and sixty nine people died

claims.text: 1983 was one of the most tense periods of the Cold War (Hoffman 1999); KAL 007 had been shot down 25 days earlier.
vo: the cold war was at its most paranoid

claims.text: The screen showed 'launch'; the system then reported a second, third, fourth and fifth missile.
vo: the screen lit up launch then a second missile a third a fourth a fifth

claims.text: His job was to report strikes up the chain to the military and political leadership, who would have had very little time to decide.
claims.caveat: Simplified chain (Hoffman 1999: warning-system HQ → general staff → Andropov). Podvig: at least three assessment layers sat above Petrov and missiles would not have been launched on satellite warning alone — hence 'might have only minutes', never 'he alone decided'.
vo: his job was to pass it up the chain
to leaders who might have only minutes to decide whether to strike back

claims.text: Lieutenant Colonel Stanislav Petrov, born 7 Sept 1939, was 44 on 26 Sept 1983.
vo: lieutenant colonel stanislav petrov

claims.text: Petrov: a funny feeling in his gut; 'when people start a war, they don't start it with only five missiles.'
claims.quote: When people start a war, they don't start it with only five missiles.
vo: had a funny feeling in his gut
when people start a war he said they don't start it with only five missiles
screen: “When people start a war, they don't start it with only five missiles.

claims.text: He reported a system malfunction (a false alarm) instead of an attack.
vo: so he reported a false alarm

claims.text: 'Twenty-three minutes later I realised that nothing had happened.'
claims.quote: Twenty-three minutes later I realised that nothing had happened.
vo: and then he waited twenty three minutes nothing came

claims.text: Cause: sunlight reflecting off high-altitude clouds in a rare sun–satellite geometry fooled the Oko satellites.
vo: it was sunlight reflecting off high clouds at a rare angle fooling a satellite

claims.text: No reward or medal; he was officially reprimanded for mistakes in the logbook (paperwork).
vo: there was no medal
he was reprimanded for incomplete paperwork
claims.caveat: Accounts differ: Hoffman (1999) says he was 'neither punished nor rewarded' after being pressed on why he hadn't written everything down; Petrov told the BBC (2013) he got an official reprimand for logbook mistakes. Narration follows his 2013 account — keep the word 'paperwork'.

claims.text: The incident became public only in 1998 (Gen. Yury Votintsev's memoirs): about fifteen years of secrecy.
vo: and the story stayed secret for fifteen years

claims.text: His wife knew nothing for ten years; 'Nothing. I did nothing.'
claims.quote: My late wife for 10 years knew nothing about it. 'So what did you do?' she asked me. 'Nothing. I did nothing.'
vo: for ten years his own wife knew nothing
when she asked what he'd done he said nothing i did nothing

claims.text: He died 19 May 2017; his death became widely known only in September 2017.
vo: he died in 2017 so quietly the world only found out months later

claims.text: Britannica: 'He is survived by his two children, two grandchildren, and the entire human race.'
claims.quote: He is survived by his two children, two grandchildren, and the entire human race.
vo: one obituary said he was survived by two children two grandchildren and the entire human race

myths.reality: He had no launch authority; he judged the alert false and reported a malfunction.

myths.myth: Petrov alone stood between the world and nuclear war.
myths.reality: At least three assessment layers sat above him (Podvig). His call still mattered: the system was built to trust its computers.

guardrails.why: He could not launch anything (see myths).
Sources conflict on which US base the false launches appeared to come from.

saturated_angles: The man who saved the world
landscape.our_gap: Told as a paper trail: the reprimand for paperwork, 15 years of secrecy, a wife who didn't know, and the obituary line. Honest that he 'reported a false alarm' (not 'refused to launch'), with Podvig's caveat built into the wording ('might have'). Every claim is cited in the description.
